texts.P-PARA-05-S01: Every classroom is in one teaching bar whose ground level houses the art and music rooms. Between this bar and the tall gym-and-dining hall stands a small front-office block containing the principal's office, nurse and maintenance, with the library on its upper level. Students reach lunch and gym only by passing through that office block, which makes oversight easy but daily trips longer. Neither the office block nor the hall reaches three stories.
texts.P-FLIP-05-S01: A single academic bar holds all classrooms, with art and music on its ground floor. A compact civic hub of administration, medical and custodial, topped by media, sits at the far end of the double-height commons, away from the bar. All movement between classrooms and the civic hub passes through the commons. This centralizes social life in the commons but lengthens daily routes to the office and nurse. The hub and commons give up the three-floor preference.
texts.P-PARA-05-S04: Nearly everything a student or visitor needs during the day, including classrooms, special education, the front office, the nurse and the library, sits in one large school building. The gym-and-cafeteria hall and a separate studio-and-maintenance building are free-standing, joined only to each other, and children walk outdoors to reach them. Keeping them separate makes evening community use and building in stages easier, but daily outdoor crossings cost supervision, shelter and a single controlled entrance.
texts.P-FLIP-05-S04: One consolidated learning house holds administration, medical, special education, classrooms and media. The commons and an arts-and-service pavilion are attached to it. They are linked to each other and reached from the house through enclosed corridors. Attaching the commons and arts makes daily supervision simpler. Students never cross open ground for lunch, gym and arts, which strengthens supervision, weather protection and single-entry control, but complicates after-hours use and phasing.
texts.P-PARA-A-E04: Apart from the gym-dining hall, both buildings are three stories tall. One is a vertical support building: front office, nurse and maintenance at street level, the special-education suite one level up, and the library at the top. The other is the teaching bar, with art and music studios at grade and classrooms on every level. Every stated floor preference is satisfied, but students in special education have no ground-level access, rely on lifts and protected stairs, and are apart from their general-education peers.
texts.P-FLIP-A-E04: Both non-commons masses rise three floors. A support tower stacks administration, medical and custodial at grade, media on floor 2 and art and music on top. Special education occupies the academic bar's ground floor beneath classrooms on all three floors. This meets the three-floor and media-above-admin preferences but gives up ground-floor arts. In exchange, special education keeps ground access and stays beside grade-level classmates.
texts.P-PARA-B-E05: The library is placed on the second level of the classroom building, so every grade passes it daily; special education sits directly beneath it at grade. A single-story front building combines the office and nurse with the art and music rooms, open to community use. Putting the library among the classrooms means it is not above the office, and the front building stays one level.
texts.P-FLIP-B-E05: Media moves out of the learning bar to the top floor of a two-story civic-arts front, above administration, as a community library rather than a daily heart for every grade. Special education stays on the ground floor of the learning bar. This case keeps the media-above-administration preference but makes media less reachable daily from classrooms. The civic-arts front gives up the three-floor preference.
texts.P-GEN-1: A welcoming, well-organized elementary school designed around student learning. Flexible classrooms, a vibrant commons and supportive spaces work together to create a safe, inclusive and inspiring environment for children, staff and the wider community, with careful attention to circulation, daylight and efficiency.
texts.P-GEN-2: The design balances the program across three masses and respects the brief's requirements and preferences. Departments are carefully allocated to support learning, community use and operations, while unresolved dimensional checks remain for later stages.
texts.P-INC-ANCHOR: Special education sits on the ground floor of the classroom bar, directly beside the grade-level classrooms it serves, so students share corridors, lunch routes and daily routines with their peers while keeping step-free access.
texts.P-INC-SAMEINTENT: To keep students with disabilities part of everyday school life, their suite is placed on the second floor of the teaching bar, interleaved with same-grade classrooms, with an elevator and refuge stair next to it.
texts.P-INC-SAMEWORDS: Special education sits on the ground floor of a separate support wing, beside the nurse and guidance offices it relies on, so students share therapy, medical and family-meeting routines with specialists while keeping step-free access.
texts.P-CIV-ANCHOR: Gym, dining and the front office form one civic mass at the main entrance, so evening community events use a single controlled door while the classroom bar can be locked off behind it.
texts.P-CIV-SAMEINTENT: For evening and weekend use, the hall and its lobby are placed in a free-standing pavilion with its own entrance and toilets; the teaching building is never opened, and staff close one gate between them.
texts.P-CIV-SAMEWORDS: Gym, dining and the front office are spread along the classroom bar at the main entrance, so evening community events pass along the main corridor and the classroom areas cannot be locked off separately.
texts.P-SRV-ANCHOR: Custodial and kitchen receiving share the commons mass, so deliveries, waste and maintenance reach food service directly without crossing student circulation.
texts.P-SRV-SAMEINTENT: Maintenance staff work from a small service yard beside the dining hall's back wall; the loading dock, bins and kitchen door are grouped there, out of sight of pupils.
texts.P-SRV-SAMEWORDS: Custodial and kitchen receiving sit in the civic hub, so deliveries, waste and maintenance reach food service by crossing the student link between hub and commons.
